subject: Political Science
title: Paper I - Classical and Enlightenment Political Thought

segments.text: Plato

asks what a genuinely just political order looks like, and links good government tightly to knowledge, moral education, and the proper ordering of society. His Republic develops justice, rule by philosopher-kings, education, and the argument that political disorder reflects disorder within individual character — he distrusts uncontrolled democracy specifically because he fears rule driven by appetite and demagoguery rather than reasoned judgment.
Aristotle

studies politics more empirically, treating the state as a natural association aimed at enabling a genuinely good life. He compares different constitutions systematically, distinguishes correct forms of government from their deviant counterparts, stresses the rule of law over arbitrary rule by individuals, and argues a large, stable middle class helps prevent extreme political instability — a useful contrast point against Plato’s more rigidly hierarchical model.
Machiavelli

studies how political power is actually acquired, preserved, and lost, rather than describing politics purely through ideal morality. The Prince emphasizes prudence, calculated force, fortune (chance beyond a ruler’s control), and political skill, judging actions by their political effect rather than abstract virtue alone — though his separate republican writings also genuinely value civic freedom and institutions, so reducing him to simply “evil politics” misses half his actual thought.
Montesquieu

explains how laws and institutions should fit the specific social conditions they govern, and how liberty can be protected specifically by preventing any single concentration of power. He is closely associated with the separation of powers and checks among distinct governmental functions, and his Spirit of the Laws stresses climate, custom, economy, and history as genuine influences on what law is appropriate for a given society.
Thomas Hobbes

begins from the deep insecurity of a condition without any common authority, and argues that lasting peace requires a very strong, largely undivided sovereign. In Leviathan, individuals authorize this sovereign through a covenant precisely because fear of violent conflict makes security society’s first political need.
John Locke

argues instead that political authority exists specifically to protect natural rights (life, liberty, and property) and remains genuinely limited by law and by the consent of the governed; if government betrays the trust its authority actually rests on, resistance can become justified.
Jean-Jacques Rousseau

asks how people can obey law while still remaining free, answering through collective self-government expressed in the “general will” — his social contract transforms mere individuals into citizens of a shared political community, and the general will concerns the genuine common good, not simply the arithmetic sum of everyone’s private preferences. These three social-contract thinkers — Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau — are best learned together as three different answers to the exact same underlying question: why should anyone accept political authority at all, and on what terms?
Immanuel Kant

connects politics with moral autonomy, republican constitutionalism, and a rule-based peace among states; his political writings defend freedom under public law and develop conditions for “perpetual peace,” including republican states forming a voluntary federation rather than any single world government — he should not be read as a simple pacifist.
J. S. Mill

defends individual liberty while allowing its restriction specifically when conduct causes genuine harm to others (the harm principle); On Liberty develops this alongside freedom of thought and individuality, while his writings on representative government discuss political participation, competence, and institutional safeguards against majority tyranny.
Jeremy Bentham

develops utilitarianism: public policy should be judged strictly by its consequences for human welfare, commonly summarized as maximizing overall happiness; he attacks vague natural-rights language as unhelpful and favours legal and institutional reform grounded in calculated utility and transparency instead — though this raises a genuine problem of how minority interests get protected under a purely aggregate utility calculation.
Hegel

sees freedom as something that develops through social institutions over time, rather than as mere freedom from external restraint. In his Philosophy of Right, family, civil society, and the state form successive stages of what he calls ethical life, and his “rational state” is not simply any existing government — it is specifically an institution in which freedom becomes objective and real through law and genuine membership in a political community, a reading that has generated real debate over whether Hegel ultimately supports constitutionalism or an excessive form of statism.

Classical and Enlightenment Thought key takeaways: Plato and Aristotle represent two different methods (ideal theory versus empirical comparison) applied to the same underlying question about the best political order. Machiavelli separates political effectiveness from conventional morality without abandoning genuine political values entirely. Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau each answer the social-contract question differently, and this contrast is the most efficient way to learn all three together. Kant extends contract-style thinking to relations between states themselves. Mill and Bentham represent two different versions of liberalism — rights-and-harm-based versus consequence-based — that can reach different conclusions on the same policy question. Hegel reframes freedom as something realized through social institutions, not simply the absence of restraint on an isolated individual.
